differences.aspect: Fit to the brief (calm, no pressure, discovery)
differences.design_x: Design X's recommended option, 'The Glasshouse Stroll', is a six-checkpoint shared-floor walk with no hazards, no time limit and no failure state; its prototype pillars are 'Always calm', 'Discover together' and 'Welcome everyone', and its flow ends gently at about 3:00.
differences.design_y: Design Y's recommended option, 'Glasshouse Garden Stroll', is a five-checkpoint shared-floor walk with no hazards, no timer and no leaderboard; its prototype pillars are 'Calm before spectacle', 'Discover together' and 'Belong in the atrium', and its flow likewise ends gently at 3:00 with time to talk about a favourite stop.
differences.evidence: Options step: both recommend a calm loop walk with submission + discovery as the listed feelings and explicitly no timer/failure. Prototype step: both carry the same pillars and a ~3 minute gentle flow. Build step: both set timeLimit to null and repeat 'no hazards and no way to fail' in the rules.

differences.design_x: Design X's build plan layout_brief requires a broad single loop around the perimeter, all scenery and route markings at least 0.6 m from the glass, and a clear 1.2 m walking width; its prototype test questions ask whether both players can pass every marker 'without crowding or approaching the glass walls'.
differences.design_y: Design Y's build plan layout_brief requires one wide gentle loop, an approximately 1.2 m clear walking route, all scenery at least 0.6 m inside the floor edges, no hazards and no dense prop clusters; its prototype decisions include 'Keep a wide unobstructed route, small props outside the walking line and all scenery clear of the real floor edges'.
differences.evidence: Build step: both layout_briefs state the same 0.6 m scenery margin and ~1.2 m walking width for the same 5 x 6 m glass atrium. Prototype step: both include decisions/test questions about two people pausing without crowding and keeping clear of edges.

differences.aspect: Specificity and buildability of the final plan
differences.design_x: Design X's build plan gives six concrete, ordered checkpoints with placement tied to the route (gate at spawn, ferns along the first edge, sunflower at the first corner, lily bridge at the next short edge, fountain at the next side, last seed near the public-facing corner) and describes each stop's content (one readable gold flower cluster, a cool blue fountain vignette with butterflies).
differences.design_y: Design Y's build plan gives five ordered checkpoints with named positions (near-left corner, far-left side, far side, far-right side, near-right side) and describes each vignette (lily pond outside the walking line, low drift of blue blossoms, modest wooden windmill with slow turning sails).
differences.evidence: Build step: Design X specifies six stops with corner/side placement and per-stop content; Design Y specifies five stops with side placement and per-stop content. Design X's checkpoint set is slightly more granular (six stops with a defined visual climax at the fountain plus a final seed and portal), while Design Y's is a little looser ('across the far side', 'on the far-right side').

differences.design_x: Design X keeps the same title, six named checkpoints, loop route, morning lighting and portal finish from options through prototype to build; the prototype's sketch zones and path match the six stops plus portal, and the build layout_brief repeats them in the same order.
differences.design_y: Design Y keeps the same title, five named stops, loop route, morning lighting and portal-near-entrance finish across all three steps; its sketch zones and path match the five stops plus portal, and the build layout_brief repeats them in order.
differences.evidence: Options -> prototype -> build: in both sessions the checkpoint names, count, route shape, lighting and finish behaviour carry through unchanged, and each prototype sketch's zones/path correspond to the same stops later restated in the build plan.

differences.aspect: Feasibility within 3 minutes for two first-time users
differences.design_x: Design X's prototype flow spaces six stops across 0:20-2:40 with short pauses and ends by about 3:00; its options step scores buildability 5 and players_fit 5 for needing no prior VR skill.
differences.design_y: Design Y's prototype flow spaces five stops across 0:20-2:35 and ends at 3:00 with time to remove headsets; its options step also scores buildability 5 and players_fit 5 for needing no controls beyond walking.
differences.evidence: Prototype step: both flows reach the portal around 2:35-2:40 and close at ~3:00. Options step: both give the recommended walk buildability 5 and players_fit 5 with the same reasoning (simple ordered checkpoints, no hazards or timer).

differences.design_x: Design X places the finish portal facing the main passing route so onlookers can cheer or ask to try next, and its spectator_plan keeps passing visitors outside the walking area with no in-game task.
differences.design_y: Design Y orients the windmill pause and arch-to-portal finish toward the glass-side edge so spectators can see the pair's reactions, and its spectator_plan keeps them beyond the edge with no guiding task.
differences.evidence: Options step: both describe spectators watching the pair stroll and finish without entering the floor. Build step: both spectator_plans state spectators stay outside the play floor and have no task, while the finale is visible to them.

differences.aspect: Range and honesty of the three options
differences.design_x: Design X offers a walk (high confidence), a chess-garden tactics idea (medium) and a gentle battle idea (low), and flags that the battle 'only partly meets the request for a calm experience with no pressure'.
differences.design_y: Design Y offers a walk (high confidence), a chess-garden tactics idea (medium) and a gentle battle idea (medium), and notes the battle 'cannot match the pure relaxation of the walking tour' and is 'the least comfortable choice for people who have never held VR controllers'.
differences.evidence: Options step: both sessions present the same three genres with the walk recommended and both explicitly warn that the battle option conflicts with the no-pressure, first-time brief.

improvements: Design X could add an explicit comfort measure like Design Y's 1-5 calm rating test question to verify the 'submission' feeling, not just readability and crowding.
Design Y could tighten positional language in the build plan (for example replace 'across the far side' with corner/edge references) to match Design X's more precise checkpoint placement.
Both could state the exact real-world anchor for the spawn/entrance relative to the atrium doors so a builder can place the loop without guessing which side is 'public-facing'.
summary: Both sessions recommend and develop essentially the same game: a calm, shared, five-to-six-stop botanical loop walk in the bright atrium with no timer, no hazards and no failure, ending at a portal near the start. They match on brief fit, safety margins, spectator handling, feasibility and step-to-step consistency. Design X's final build plan is marginally more specific about checkpoint placement and per-stop content (six stops tied to corners/edges with a defined fountain climax), while Design Y is equally coherent but a touch looser in positional language. The difference is small and does not change what players experience, so this is a tie.
why: On every aspect that matters to the creator or players - fit to the calm/no-pressure brief, safety margins in the glass atrium, consistency between options, prototype and build, feasibility in three minutes, and spectator handling - the two sessions are equivalent. The only real difference is that Design X's build plan pins its six checkpoints to slightly more precise locations and content than Design Y's five, which is a minor specificity edge but not enough to prefer one design overall.
x_weaknesses: Design X's test questions focus on comprehension, crowding and readability but do not include a direct measure of whether players actually feel calmer, whereas Design Y asks for a 1-5 calm rating.
Design X's six stops in three minutes leaves slightly less unhurried time per stop than Design Y's five, which could matter for the 'submission' feeling.
y_weaknesses: Design Y's build plan uses looser positional language for some checkpoints ('across the far side', 'on the far-right side') compared with Design X's corner/edge-anchored placement.
Design Y's prototype prompt_style mentions 'warm afternoon sun' while everywhere else it specifies morning lighting, a small internal inconsistency.
